story.headline: Federal court upholds climate-blockade fines
story.summary: Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court confirmed suspended fines for Extinction Rebellion activists who blockaded a Zurich street in 2021, ruling free expression is no justification.
story.display_body: Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court ruled on Wednesday 26 August that climate activists who blockaded a Zurich street can be criminally punished, holding that freedom of expression is no justification for the blockade. In a series of judgments published Wednesday, the Bundesgericht (the country's highest court) confirmed the suspended fines imposed for coercion (Nötigung) on several Extinction Rebellion activists who, on 4 October 2021, joined roughly 200 protesters occupying central Zurich's Uraniastrasse and sat in the road for about an hour and a half — ignoring repeated police orders to clear it — until police forcibly removed them. The court rejected the activists' argument that their convictions breached their rights to free expression and assembly: it stressed that free expression is a very high value and that authorities must show some tolerance even toward unauthorised gatherings — and noted Zurich police had indeed initially let the protest proceed — but found the activists had "overstepped," because the decisive factors are the scale and duration of a disruption and how severely uninvolved people are affected in their daily lives.
story.why: this sets a national precedent on the limits of protest in Switzerland — demonstrations may be disruptive and inconvenient, but blocking traffic for extended periods gives activists no legal "free pass," a line that will shape how future climate and other protests are policed and prosecuted.

story.headline: EU packaging rules squeeze Swiss exporters
story.summary: The EU's new packaging regulation, in force since 12 August, imposes heavy registration costs on small exporters, including Swiss micro-businesses.
story.display_body: A new EU packaging regulation in force since 12 August is imposing outsized compliance costs on small exporters, Swiss micro-businesses among them, Le Temps reported on Wednesday 26 August. The EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (PPWR — the bloc's overhauled rules meant to cut packaging waste and push a "circular economy") now requires sellers shipping goods into EU countries to register, declare and pay fees for the packaging they put on each national market. For very small players the paperwork dwarfs the volumes involved: Patrick Hufschmid, an independent luthier (stringed-instrument maker) based in Aigle (Vaud) who mails guitar plectrums to EU customers in stiff cardboard envelopes, told the paper he now faces close to €260 a year in compliance fees plus separate registrations, declarations and compliance bodies for each country — just to ship under two kilos of cardboard annually to France and Germany.
story.why: Switzerland is outside the EU but its exporters must still meet the bloc's rules to sell there, so an EU regulation aimed at large-scale waste lands as a disproportionate administrative burden on Swiss artisans and micro-enterprises — a concrete example of how EU single-market rules reach across the border into Swiss working life.

story.headline: SBB half-year profit more than doubles
story.summary: Swiss Federal Railways reported a first-half 2026 profit of 126 million francs, up from 48 million a year earlier, with freight breaking even.
story.display_body: Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) reported on Wednesday 26 August that its first-half 2026 profit more than doubled to 126 million francs, from 48 million a year earlier, as ridership rose. An average of 1.45 million passengers travelled with SBB each day in the half; punctuality slipped slightly to 94.1% (down 0.4 points on H1 2025), while customer satisfaction edged up to 80.1 points. The railway credited higher passenger demand, a positive real-estate result and an improved freight performance — SBB Cargo's result rose by 49 million francs to a 2-million-franc profit, its first roughly balanced result in many years. SBB cautioned that its finances remain demanding: to renew its large vehicle fleets and expand service it says it needs a profit of around 500 million francs a year in the medium term to stabilise its debt.
story.why: SBB is a federally owned backbone of Swiss daily life, and the profit jump — set against the much larger sum the company says it actually needs — is a marker of both a recovering post-pandemic demand and the long-term funding gap facing the network reader-taxpayers ultimately underwrite.

story.headline: Islamabad hospital fire kills 14 newborns
story.summary: A fire in a maternity ward at PIMS hospital in Islamabad killed at least 14 infants on Wednesday morning.
story.display_body: A fire in a maternity ward at a public hospital in Islamabad killed at least 14 newborns early on Wednesday 26 August, Pakistani authorities said. The blaze broke out around 6:45 a.m. local time on the third floor — the MCH (maternal and child health) ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) — when, according to rescuers, an air-conditioning unit exploded inside the nursery. Officials said 16 newborns were in the ward at the time and that one was rescued; a nurse read out the names of the dead outside the hospital. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ordered an immediate investigation.
story.why: it is a catastrophic failure of basic safety in a flagship state hospital, and the death of newborns in a supposedly protected ward points to the fragility of public-health infrastructure in one of the world's most populous countries.

story.headline: Ukraine strikes stall Russian grain exports
story.summary: Intensified Ukrainian drone attacks on Novorossiysk and other Black Sea ports are disrupting Russian grain and oil exports.
story.display_body: Intensified Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia's Black Sea ports are now disrupting Russian grain and oil exports, not just military targets, DW reported on Tuesday 25 August. Strikes in recent weeks on Novorossiysk — Russia's largest commercial Black Sea port and a hub for both grain and crude — have caused significant disruption to shipments, part of a widening Ukrainian campaign against the ports and refineries that fund Moscow's war. Ukraine's deep strikes have already pushed the Russian navy off its former dominance of the northwestern Black Sea; the new element is the reach into commercial export flows.
story.why: Novorossiysk is a major artery for globally traded grain and oil, so a sustained hit to it raises the risk of ripple effects on world food and energy prices — turning a battlefield tactic into a pressure point on markets far from the front.

story.headline: Haiti attack toll rises to 47
story.summary: The UN confirmed at least 47 killed and more than 50 kidnapped in a gang attack near Port-au-Prince on Sunday.
story.display_body: The UN confirmed on Tuesday 25 August that at least 47 people, including at least five children, were killed and more than 50 kidnapped in a gang attack near Haiti's capital — a sharply higher toll than the ~40 first reported. The raid struck Kenscoff, in the hills above Port-au-Prince, on Sunday 23 August; the UN now calls it one of the largest mass kidnappings in the troubled Caribbean country in recent years, and Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack. Survivors, many of them already displaced by earlier violence, fled with whatever belongings they could carry.
story.why: the confirmed scale — and the mass abductions on top of the killings — underscores how far gang control has spread around the Haitian capital and how little protection the state can offer displaced civilians.

story.headline: WHO urges distancing as Ebola spreads in DRC
story.summary: The WHO recommended social-distancing measures in the DRC to counter the country's deadliest recorded Ebola outbreak.
story.display_body: The World Health Organization on Monday 24 August recommended social-distancing measures in the Democratic Republic of Congo to slow the country's deadliest-ever recorded Ebola outbreak. After an emergency-committee meeting last week, WHO director-general Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus issued recommendations that the DRC postpone large gatherings and limit motorcycle taxis to a single passenger in transmission zones, alongside stronger surveillance, case management, community mobilisation and protection of health workers. (Ebola is a severe, often-fatal haemorrhagic fever spread through contact with the bodily fluids of infected people.)
story.why: reaching for social-distancing and mobility limits — tools associated with respiratory pandemics — signals that responders judge case-finding and vaccination alone insufficient to contain this outbreak, and that everyday movement in affected areas is now part of the control strategy.
